Article Title: A Utah couple wanted a place to scuba without travelling, so they built a $2 million, 360,000-gallon backyard pool with a 90-foot mountain, five waterfalls, a 300-foot lazy river and a 26-foot-deep di
Article Text:
Photo: Crazy World

A 90-foot mountain in the backyard

A tunnel that lets the owners practise scuba diving

Photo: Crazy World

A kitchen, bridges and hidden spaces

A $2 million project featured on television

A Utah couple wanted a place where they could practise scuba diving without travelling to the ocean. Their solution was to build a $2 million backyard swimming pool with 360,000 gallons of water, a 90-foot man-made mountain, five waterfalls and an underwater tunnel that takes divers down to a depth of 26 feet. Called “The Mountain”, the pool was built at a home in Springville, Utah. It stretches 140 feet long and 60 feet wide, and includes a 300-foot lazy river, a hidden grotto, winding pathways and a water slide concealed inside the mountain.As reported by FOX 13 News, the unusual pool was featured on Animal Planet’s television programme ‘The Pool Master,’ hosted by pool designer Anthony Archer-Wills. The project was designed for a homeowner who loved mountains and scuba diving, the broadcaster reported.The pool’s main feature is a 90-foot artificial mountain designed to resemble the natural landscape around the property. It includes five waterfalls, several hidden pathways and two bridges that wind towards the top. Archer-Wills described the structure as one that “emulates the natural surroundings perfectly”, according to FOX 13 News. The mountain is not just decorative. A hidden water slide runs for 60 feet through the structure before dropping into the pool below.There is also a secluded grotto tucked behind the waterfalls, giving swimmers another place to explore. The pool’s design combines these features with a 300-foot lazy river, allowing the owners to swim, float and explore different parts of the property without leaving home.Scuba diving was one of the main reasons the couple commissioned the pool. Utah is far from the ocean, so having a deep-water area at home offered them a place to practise. According to FOX 13 News, a concealed entrance inside the mountain leads to a tunnel measuring 54 feet long and five feet wide. The tunnel reaches a depth of 26 feet and connects to the main pool. The underwater section is intended for scuba-certified divers. It allows them to put on diving equipment and practise underwater skills without travelling to a coastal diving location. As reported by Scuba Diving magazine, the $2 million project included the 54-foot tunnel, five waterfalls, the lazy river and a hidden 60-foot slide in the year 2014.The pool also has facilities for spending time outdoors beyond swimming and diving. According to FOX 13 News, the mountain houses a full kitchen with granite countertops, stainless-steel cabinets, a refrigerator and an eight-burner grill. The bridges and paths offer access to the upper sections of the structure, while the hidden grotto and winding passages give the mountain several enclosed spaces to explore. The combination of water features, diving facilities and kitchen space makes the backyard pool more elaborate than a conventional residential swimming pool.The project came to wider attention when it appeared on ‘The Pool Master,’ a programme that follows pool designer Anthony Archer-Wills as he transforms residential outdoor spaces. The pool cost approximately $2 million to build. In its 2015 report, Scuba Diving magazine highlighted the project as an example of how a private swimming pool could be designed around a specific hobby. For the Utah homeowners, the central purpose was practical as well as recreational: they wanted somewhere to practise scuba diving close to home. The result was a 360,000-gallon pool built around an artificial mountain, with five waterfalls, a lazy river, a hidden slide and a 26-foot-deep underwater tunnel.
Article Summary: A Utah couple wanted a place where they could practise scuba diving without travelling to the ocean. Their solution was to build a $2 million backyard pool with 360,000 gallons of water, a 90-foot man-made mountain, five waterfalls and an underwater tunnel. Called ‘The Mountain’, the pool was built at a home in Springville, Utah. It stretches 140 feet long and 60 feet wide, and includes a 300-foot lazy river, a hidden grotto, winding pathways and a water slide concealed inside the mountain.

Article Title: ​Florida permanently protects nearly 1,500 acres across two cattle ranches with $8.7 million in conservation easements, preventing future development while preserving farmland and wildlife
Article Text:
Mossy Island

Florida Commission Company Ranch

What is the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program?

Florida has added two more ranches to its growing list of protected agricultural lands, with nearly 1,500 acres in Manatee and Highlands counties secured from future development. The ranches are now permanently protected through the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services’ Rural and Family Lands Protection Program, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture Wilton Simpson said in a release. These rural land easements prevent future development while allowing agricultural operations to continue and contribute to Florida’s economy and the production of food, timber and other resources vital to the state’s prosperity.“I’m proud to announce today the preservation of two additional working Florida agricultural operations, which builds on the historic progress we’ve made through the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program,” Commissioner Wilton Simpson said in a statement. “My goal is to secure the permanent future of agriculture in Florida, and the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program gives us the most effective and cost-efficient way to preserve our natural lands from development while also supporting our farmers and ranchers.Since the program began, Florida has protected more than 253,000 acres of farmland, including nearly 188,000 acres under Commissioner Simpson’s administration. The newly protected properties lie within the Florida Wildlife Corridor and are enrolled in the department’s Best Management Practices (BMP) programme.Mossy Island covers about 420 acres used for cattle farming, and its location does much of the work. It sits next to Myakka River State Park to the west and Myakka Prairie Conservation Easements to the south, so it already borders protected land. The surrounding area consists mostly of pasture, with some cropland and scattered low-density housing. Mossy Island is protected from future development through a $4 million conservation agreement, with $500,000 contributed by Manatee County.The state’s announcement also points to the threat. Land along the property’s northern boundary is projected to be developed by 2040, according to University of Florida projections. The easement is intended to prevent that development.Florida Commission Company Ranch sits in Highlands County and covers about 1,046 acres. The farmland is now permanently protected from development through a rural land protection easement totalling $4.7 million. The ranch raises cattle on pastures and natural areas and grows hay for on-site use.In 2001, Florida established the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program Act, which recognises the importance of working agricultural lands to the state’s economic future. This helps preserve farmland as development puts increasing pressure on rural areas. The programme works with farmers and ranchers to keep agricultural land in use and protect natural resources.The state pays landowners to restrict future development under conservation agreements, but not to stop farming and ranching. This allows the land to continue producing food and timber while also helping the state avoid the long-term costs of buying and managing conservation land itself.Since 2022, Commissioner Wilton Simpson has helped secure more than $1.1 billion in state funding for the programme, including $425 million in the 2026–27 state budget. Simpson has also played a key role in Florida’s land conservation policy long before becoming the state’s Commissioner of Agriculture. During his tenure as Senate President, he backed the Florida Wildlife Corridor Act, which aims to connect and protect natural habitats across the state while keeping working agricultural lands safe from future development.Meanwhile, Mossy Island and Florida Commission Company Ranch sit within that corridor. Both are enrolled in the state’s Best Management Practices programme, a set of environmental practices for working land. The easements protect the land from development, while the ranchers continue farming under those practices.
Article Summary: Florida has added two more ranches to its growing list of protected agricultural lands, with nearly 1,500 acres in Manatee and Highlands counties secured from future development. The ranches are now permanently protected through the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services’ Rural and Family Lands Protection Program.

Article Title: Demi Moore’s Idaho home has a river for swimming and kayaking, mountains nearby, and wild elk that sometimes wander into her backyard
Article Text:
PC: Wikipedia

What makes the river at the base of Demi Moore’s Idaho property special

How do mountains, rivers and wildlife shape life around Demi Moore’s Idaho home

Why did Demi Moore’s family turn their Idaho holiday spot into a home

What makes Sun Valley appealing to Demi Moore beyond its natural scenery

Demi Moore’s Idaho home brings her close to the natural landscape of Sun Valley, where a river, mountains, and open surroundings shape life beyond Los Angeles. She lives in Hailey, one of three connected towns in the Sun Valley area, which she says feels cosy and familiar, with little main streets, mountains, and clean air.A river runs along the base of her property, giving her a place to swim, kayak, raft, and fly-fish during summer. The surrounding landscape also brings wildlife close to home, with Moore saying she might see a herd of elk in her backyard. In a 2023 interview with the Financial Times, Moore shared how the river and its outdoor activities form part of her life in Idaho.One of the most distinctive features of Moore’s property is the river at its base. The actress described it as a popular place to spend time during the summer, particularly when the weather makes outdoor activities appealing. She says they sometimes swim there when they’re brave enough, calling the spot the “Redneck Riviera”.The river also provides opportunities for kayaking, river-rafting, and fly-fishing. These activities make the water an important part of how Moore and those who join her enjoy the warmer months.Rather than being limited to a view of the landscape, the river offers a place to get into the water and spend time outdoors.Moore’s description of life in Idaho highlights how wildlife can appear close to her home. Speaking about the natural surroundings, she said she might see a herd of elk in her backyard. Her words describe a possibility rather than a regular occurrence, but they show how the landscape around her property brings her close to the region’s wildlife.The river, mountains, and open surroundings contribute to the appeal of the area. For Moore, the setting offers a different atmosphere from Los Angeles, where she also spends time. Her description focuses on the space to breathe and the natural environment that surrounds her Idaho home.Moore said her connection to Sun Valley began through her former husband, Bruce Willis, who wanted a place there. She had not heard much about the area before her first visit, which took place when their eldest daughter, Rumer, was just 12 days old.The family initially intended to use the property as a holiday spot. When Rumer was approaching school age, however, Moore began questioning why they were staying in Los Angeles. She says that these days she splits her time between Los Angeles and Idaho. Moore said the area feels familiar because she grew up in a small town. She also values its main streets, beautiful mountains, clean air, and family-owned businesses.Moore lives in Hailey, one of three connected towns in the Sun Valley area, alongside Ketchum and Bellevue. She described the region as rustic but also cosmopolitan, with an art community and gallery walks that connect local galleries several times a year.The area also changes considerably with the seasons. Moore described summer as a blanket of green and winter as a blanket of white. In winter, she says they tend to stay indoors and play games like Mexican Train dominoes. Her former husband, Bruce Willis, and his wife, Emma, live about a mile away, according to Moore. The actress also enjoys watching British crime dramas at home.
Article Summary: Demi Moore lives in Hailey, one of three connected towns in the Sun Valley area. A river runs along the base of her property, giving her a place to swim, kayak, raft, and fly-fish during summer. The surrounding landscape also brings wildlife close to home, with Moore saying she might see a herd of elk in her backyard.

Article Title: An Ohio boy asked his dad for a baseball field in their backyard; two years and about $30,000 later, the family had its own diamond with infield clay, regulation bases, a raised mound and hand-painted
Article Text:
By the time the main construction was completed, Kidd had spent approximately $30,000 (Screengrab: Youtube/WSLS 10 News)

The biggest expenses came before the field was built

Neighbours raised concerns about the backyard project

More additions were planned for the baseball field

An Ohio father spent nearly two years and around $30,000 building a baseball field in his backyard after his five-year-old son asked whether they could have one at home.Jason Kidd, who lived in Brookfield, transformed part of his property into a playing field, with regulation bases, a raised pitcher's mound, professional-grade infield clay and foul lines that he painted himself. The project that involved extensive land preparation, eventually attracted complaints from some neighbours, WSLS 10 News reported in 2019.Kidd's son was playing with a T-ball set when he made the request, which his father initially dismissed. But the idea stayed with Kidd, who began considering whether the family had enough space for a baseball field.The father, who owned a small aircraft management business, eventually started measuring his backyard. The property was not immediately suitable for a playing field and needed a lot of preparation.By the time the main construction was completed, Kidd had spent approximately $30,000. Although the amount was considerable, he said it was close to what he had expected, and worth it to spend time with his son and introduce him to baseball.Preparing the property turned out to be one of the most demanding parts of the project.Kidd could not begin laying the playing surface until he had cleared the space and changed the existing landscape.The backyard contained numerous trees, while a hill occupied part of the area intended for the field. Both had to be removed before construction could proceed. Kidd later identified tree removal and insulation work as two of the largest expenses.The baseball surface accounted for only a fraction of the total spending. Kidd estimated that the clay cost between $5,000 and $6,000. Rather than using ordinary soil, he selected the type of material used on major league baseball fields."The field itself wasn't the most expensive," Kidd told Yahoo Lifestyle. "It was five or six thousand dollars worth of clay, the same kind of clay they use on actual big league fields," he added.The completed playing area included regulation bases and a raised pitcher's mound. Kidd also took responsibility for painting the straight foul lines himself.However, the $30,000 expenditure did not cover everything he wanted. A fence was still missing, even though he had expected it to be included within the original budget.While neighbourhood children were excited about using the field, some residents were less enthusiastic. One concern involved the possible effect on surrounding property values. Kidd recalled that a passer-by had made a negative remark to the contractors working at his home.Another neighbour questioned whether rain could carry material from the playing surface into a nearby ditch. Kidd disagreed with that concern, maintaining that the clay covering the field was too heavy to be washed away in the manner suggested.There were also worries about balls travelling beyond the playing area and breaking windows. Kidd said the field would be used for softball rather than hardball games.The complaints were not limited to conversations with neighbours. According to Kidd, a Brookfield Township trustee had received an anonymous complaint about the project.Despite completing the main playing area, Kidd had not finished all the improvements he wanted to make. His plans included a warning track, a fence and a scoreboard.Installing the fence had become a logistical problem. Arranging for steel supplies and fencing contractors to be available together was proving difficult. In July 2019, Kidd said he hoped the work could be completed within the next few weeks.Kidd, a divorced father who shared custody of his son, wanted a place where they could play together and where he could teach the boy about baseball.He was also realistic about how long his son's enthusiasm might last. At five, the boy was interested in baseball, but Kidd recognised that children often change their minds about what they want to do.He explained that his son had already expressed interest in becoming a police officer, a doctor and even a superhero. If baseball eventually stopped being important to him, Kidd said he would accept that. "If he never wants to play a professional sport, that's fine," he said.
Article Summary: Jason Kidd, who lived in Brookfield, Ohio, transformed part of his property into a playing field. The project that involved extensive land preparation, attracted complaints from some neighbours. By the time the main construction was completed, Kidd had spent approximately $30,000.

Article Title: A New Jersey mother’s 1996 will split her estate equally among four children; after her daughter became sole caregiver and a family rift, a new will cut out both sons, and an appeals court has now uph
Article Text:
A New Jersey mother removed both sons from her will in 2016 after their relationship deteriorated. (AI image)

A family rift, a new will and a legal challenge

Sons believe their mother was influenced

Why did the court uphold the mother's decision?

A New Jersey mother who once planned to leave her property equally to her four children later decided that her two sons would receive nothing. She made the change in 2016, following a breakdown in their relationship, while one of her daughters had been caring for her for years. After the woman died in 2024, the sons challenged her decision in court, claiming their sisters had influenced her. However, on Friday, a New Jersey appeals court upheld the revised will, finding insufficient evidence that the mother had been pressured into changing it.According to details of the case published by Law.com, the woman signed the will in 1996. At the time, she wanted her estate divided equally among her two sons and two daughters. She also chose one son and one daughter to handle her affairs after her death jointly.That same year, her daughter Deborah became her sole caregiver and began living in the family home. Over the following years, Deborah continued looking after her mother, while relations between the woman and her sons eventually deteriorated.The situation changed in 2015 after a family altercation. The mother's relationship with her sons became strained, and in some periods, they reportedly had no contact.A year later, she signed another will that excluded both sons, and Deborah was also named the sole person responsible for handling the estate after her mother's death.The disagreement over this decision did not reach court immediately. The mother continued living for another eight years, during which questions were raised about whether someone close to her was taking advantage of her financially.In 2021, New Jersey's Adult Protective Services Programme investigated a complaint alleging financial exploitation. The investigation did not find evidence to substantiate the allegation, and the matter was closed.When the mother died in 2024, one of her sons objected to the revised will. Both sons subsequently challenged the arrangements, questioning whether their mother had made the decision independently.Their argument focused largely on the relationships she shared with her daughters. Deborah had been her caregiver since 1996, and the mother was also close to her other daughter. The sons believed these circumstances raised doubts about whether she had acted entirely of her own choice.The sons argued that their mother's dependence on Deborah for care, together with her close relationship with their other sister, should have prompted greater scrutiny of the 2016 will. They wanted the court to require their sisters to demonstrate that their mother had not been improperly influencedThe daughters rejected these claims. They maintained that there was no evidence their mother had been controlled or persuaded to change her will against her wishes.The court examined the family's history, including the mother's deteriorating relationship with her sons and the circumstances in which she had prepared the revised document.One important detail was that neither daughter had initiated the preparation of the 2016 will. Neither was present when their mother signed it.The court also considered whether the mother had been capable of making her own decisions at the time. No medical evidence from that period showed that her ability to understand or manage her affairs had been impaired.The judge who first heard the case found that the mother's relationship with her sons had already been damaged for years before her death. The 2016 will was also consistent with decisions she made later about her estate.The court did not accept that Deborah's role as caregiver automatically meant she had control over her mother's financial decisions.The sons appealed, but the New Jersey Superior Court's Appellate Division reached the same conclusion.In its October 16 ruling, the appeals court found that the brothers had failed to provide sufficient evidence that either sister had improperly influenced their mother. It also agreed that there was no basis to require the daughters to prove the absence of such influence.The judges considered the mother's ability to manage her own affairs, the absence of evidence of pressure when the revised will was signed and the history of her relationships with her children.
Article Summary: A New Jersey mother removed both sons from her will in 2016 after their relationship deteriorated. The sons challenged her decision in court, claiming their sisters had influenced her. A New Jersey appeals court upheld the revised will, finding insufficient evidence that the mother had been pressured into changing it.

Article Title: A working mom started a party-rental side hustle with just $500 and four yard games; within months, Vanessa Romano grew it to 65 bookings and more than $9,000 in revenue without quitting her full-time
Article Text:
From a small experiment to a growing business

Managing a business alongside a full-time job

Why she is not leaving her corporate career

Starting a business does not always require a large investment or a decision to leave a stable job. For Vanessa Romano, a 39-year-old mother of two, a modest $500 investment in four outdoor party games became the foundation of a growing event-rental business. According to PEOPLE, which profiled Romano on October 12, 2026, her venture, Little Party Co., secured 65 bookings and generated more than $9,000 in booked revenue within its first few months. Romano, who works full-time in corporate communications, launched the business after noticing how party-rental ventures were gaining traction on social media. The idea appealed to her because she could start small, test whether customers were interested and retain the games for her family’s own celebrations if the business did not work out. Rather than investing heavily in equipment or renting commercial premises, she began with four yard games. The relatively low initial cost allowed her to experiment with the business while keeping her regular income intact.The response was encouraging from the outset. Little Party Co. received five bookings in its first month, generating more than $800 in revenue, enough to recover the initial inventory investment.The following month, 17 bookings brought in more than $1,800. As enquiries increased, Romano began reinvesting the earnings into the business instead of treating the money as additional personal income. Her total investment eventually reached approximately $4,500, while booked revenue climbed to more than $9,000.The growth reflects a practical approach to building a small business: begin with a limited range of products, assess demand and expand only when there is evidence that customers want more. Romano has also learned to be selective about new purchases. Rather than continuously adding equipment to make the rental collection look more impressive, she tracks bookings, considers seasonal demand and prioritises items that customers are actively seeking. This approach helps her manage costs while making decisions about which products could generate enough bookings to justify their purchase.Running Little Party Co. has brought a different set of challenges beyond attracting customers. Romano manages bookings, prepares equipment, cleans and transports the games, and coordinates collections and deliveries around her corporate responsibilities and family commitments. According to her account in PEOPLE, around three-quarters of customers collect their rentals themselves, while the remaining quarter opt for delivery. Depending on the week, she handles between two and eight clients.The physical demands can also be unpredictable. Romano has described fracturing a toe after dropping a cornhole board on her foot, yet still having to complete deliveries that day. The experience illustrates a common difficulty for solo entrepreneurs: when the owner is also responsible for operations, taking time off can be complicated. Time, rather than the initial investment, has become one of her biggest constraints. Growing the business requires work outside her regular office hours, often competing with family time and the need to rest.Despite the early success, Romano does not see Little Party Co. as a replacement for her full-time job. She has said she enjoys her corporate career and wants to continue building the rental business alongside it. Her husband has also played an important role in making the arrangement possible, taking on additional household responsibilities while she establishes the venture. For Romano, the business offers a way to pursue her entrepreneurial interests while creating greater financial flexibility for her family.Her experience also reflects a broader appeal of rental-based businesses: equipment can be used repeatedly to generate bookings rather than being sold just once. However, revenue alone does not establish profitability, as expenses such as maintenance, transportation, storage, replacement equipment and taxes must also be considered. Romano's story is a reminder that entrepreneurship does not always have to begin with an all-or-nothing decision. Starting with a small inventory, reinvesting earnings and responding to customer demand allowed her to test a business idea without giving up the security of a regular salary. For now, she is choosing to grow both careers rather than abandon one for the other.
Article Summary: Vanessa Romano, a 39-year-old mother of two, launched Little Party Co. after noticing how party-rental ventures were gaining traction on social media. Rather than investing heavily in equipment or renting commercial premises, she began with four yard games. The relatively low initial cost allowed her to experiment with the business while keeping her regular income intact.

Article Title: A 12-year-old boy was beside his mother when she passed out while driving at 60 mph, grabbed the wheel and stopped the car before calling 999; now 13, Zac Howells has won a Pride of Britain courage aw
Article Text:
Zac Howells will receive the Child of Courage Award at London’s Pride of Britain Awards, honouring his extraordinary bravery.

A routine journey takes a frightening turn

A split-second decision

Staying focused after the crash

A hero in the eyes of his family

For most children, a car journey with a parent is an ordinary part of the day. For Zac Howells, one December drive suddenly became a test of instinct, courage and extraordinary composure. At just 12, he found himself trying to control a moving car after his mother lost consciousness behind the wheel. What happened next helped avert what could have been a devastating crash. According to an online report by AOL, now 13, Zac is being recognised with the Child of Courage Award at the Pride of Britain Awards for his actions that day, which not only protected him and his mother but potentially prevented other road users from being caught in a serious accident.According to an AOL report, last December, Zac was travelling with his mother, Nicola Crump, from their home in Ebbw Vale towards a Christmas market in Warwickshire. The journey had begun like any other, with the pair listening to music as Nicola drove along the A40 in Herefordshire. They were travelling at around 60mph when Nicola began to feel unwell. She managed to slow the car and guide it partly onto a narrow verge.Within moments, however, she lost consciousness.The situation became even more dangerous because the automatic car remained in drive. With Nicola's foot still on the accelerator, the vehicle began moving back towards the dual carriageway and gathering speed. Zac immediately realised that something was seriously wrong.As per the report, the 12-year-old had no time to wait for help. He reached across from the passenger seat and grabbed the steering wheel, attempting to keep the vehicle under control as it moved towards the central reservation. He steered the car towards the barrier, using it to slow the vehicle until it finally came to a halt. He then switched off the engine and called 999. In the middle of the chaos, Zac also used the car's satnav to establish their location, giving emergency services the information they needed to reach them quickly, adds another report by The Forester.The decision to use the central reservation as a means of stopping the vehicle came with its own risks, but it prevented the car from continuing into the road or potentially leaving the carriageway, adds the online report.The danger did not end when the car stopped. Nicola remained unconscious for around seven minutes, leaving Zac to deal with the aftermath while waiting for police and paramedics, claims the report by AOL.Emergency responders later found that Nicola had suffered extremely low blood pressure. She is undergoing further cardiology investigations and has not yet returned to driving, informs the AOL report.For Zac, the experience was understandably terrifying. Yet those who responded to the emergency were struck by how composed he remained. His 999 call captured the seriousness of the situation, but also his immediate concern for his mother. That combination of clear thinking and compassion became a defining part of the story.When Nicola regained consciousness, she saw emergency lights approaching and was initially confused about what had happened. Zac was physically trembling but remained focused on reassuring her. For his mother, the incident has brought home just how extraordinary his actions were. A journey that began as a simple trip to a Christmas market could easily have ended very differently. Zac's bravery will now be formally recognised at the Pride of Britain Awards, where he will receive the Child of Courage Award at a ceremony at Grosvenor House in London on October 19.Image Courtesy: The Forester
Article Summary: Zac Howells will receive the Child of Courage Award at London’s Pride of Britain Awards, honouring his extraordinary bravery. At just 12, he found himself trying to control a moving car after his mother lost consciousness behind the wheel. What happened next helped avert what could have been a devastating crash.

Article Title: 'Don’t trust anybody': Trump's response to Netanyahu question ahead of Israel polls
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump says he “doesn’t trust anybody” in politics when asked about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while stopping short of committing to an endorsement ahead of Israel’s October 27 election

Iran tensions add to election uncertainty

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he does not trust anyone in politics when asked whether he trusts Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as speculation continues over Washington’s role in Israel’s October 27 election.“I don’t trust anybody, honestly,” Trump told right-wing cable news outlet Newsmax. “In the world of politics I don’t trust anybody.”Trump was also asked whether he planned to campaign for Netanyahu, who has frequently highlighted his close relationship with the US president during election campaigns.“Well, they’d like me to be. Yeah, they’d like me to be,” Trump said, referring to Israeli officials who want him to get involved in Netanyahu’s re-election campaign.He nevertheless described his relationship with the Israeli prime minister as “very good” and praised their “very successful… military partnership” against Iran.Trump has repeatedly declined to commit to endorsing Netanyahu ahead of the Israeli election, which comes amid heightened tensions over Iran’s nuclear programme and the possibility of renewed military action.Netanyahu and Trump reportedly discussed the possibility of a joint US-Israeli operation against Iran amid Israeli concerns that Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear programme, according to an Axios report citing US and Israeli officials and other sources familiar with the discussions.The report said Netanyahu had held several calls with Trump over two weeks about potentially resuming major combat operations against Iran. The discussions reportedly included possible strikes on Iranian military and nuclear facilities.However, the White House disputed the account, calling the claim that Trump and Netanyahu had discussed resuming the war “false”. A White House official said Trump had made clear that the US would not attack Iran before the American midterm elections.Netanyahu’s office said the Israeli prime minister remained in regular contact with Trump and senior US officials but did not comment on the substance of their conversations.With Israel scheduled to vote on October 27 and US midterm elections approaching, any renewed military campaign against Iran could carry political consequences for both leaders. The prospect of Iranian retaliation has also raised concerns about the potential disruption of Israel’s election process.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump says he ‘doesn’t trust anybody’ in politics when asked about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump stopped short of committing to an endorsement ahead of Israel’s October 27 election. Netanyahu has frequently highlighted his close relationship with the US president during election campaigns.

Article Title: Explosion, fuel leak: Two Syrian pipelines damaged in fresh blow to war-hit energy network
Article Text:
Security forces of Syria's Interior Ministry guard the al-Omar oil field, the country's largest by area and production

Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday, with one explosion triggering a fire and another causing a fuel leak, Syrian state media reported.According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), citing the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, an explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in Hasakah province, while a separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.The explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze.The Syrian Petroleum Company described the incident as sabotage. Officials said alternative arrangements would maintain gas supplies to power stations during repairs, while domestic gas supplies remained unaffected.In a separate incident, a hole was discovered in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area west of Homs, causing a leak of petroleum products. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to contain the leak and isolate the damaged section.Al Jazeera, citing Syrian state media, reported that the damage to the Baniyas-Homs pipeline was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft. The initial reports did not confirm the cause or identify those responsible.The incidents come amid a series of disruptions to Syria’s energy infrastructure. Earlier in October, an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in Hasakah province was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage.Syria is working to rebuild its oil and gas infrastructure after years of conflict, restoring production in northeastern oilfields and reconnecting them with processing facilities and refineries in Homs and Baniyas.In January 2026, the Syrian Petroleum Company began pumping raw gas from the Jbessa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs countryside at around 1.2 million cubic metres per day to support electricity generation.The second damaged pipeline, connecting Baniyas on the Mediterranean coast to Homs, transports petroleum products between two important energy centres. The Baniyas refinery is undergoing an overhaul aimed at increasing its processing capacity from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.Syria has also undertaken emergency pipeline repairs and plans to expand its transportation network. A September 2026 analysis by the Baker Institute for Public Policy reported that the Syrian Petroleum Company was repairing existing infrastructure and planning a heavy-crude pipeline linking northeastern oilfields to the Baniyas refinery.
Article Summary: Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday. One explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze. A separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.

Article Title: ‘Couldn’t wait to kill Indians’: US teen’s neo-Nazi manifesto reveals Hindu temple attack plot
Article Text:
File photo: Alexandros Paporakis, 19, has been charged over an alleged mass shooting plot that may have targeted a Hindu place of worship near Chicago

Planning attack for 2 years

Gun allegedly jammed during visit to temple

Rifle, ammunition and Nazi imagery recovered

Arrest renews concern over anti-Indian hate

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the most effective way to prevent hate-driven attacks? Stronger law enforcement and security Education and awareness against hate Early reporting of extremist threats 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A 19-year-old US man who allegedly told co-workers he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” was arrested over a suspected mass shooting plot targeting a Hindu temple in Aurora, near Chicago. Police say he had shared a racist manifesto and visited the temple on the day investigators believe he planned to attack.Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from Palatine, Illinois, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches. A judge ordered him detained before trial on Wednesday. His next court appearance is scheduled for October 30.According to prosecutors, Paporakis openly identified himself as a white supremacist at work and regularly made disparaging remarks about people of different races, including Indians. His colleagues told investigators that he discussed Nazis and violence and that his behaviour had intensified in the days before his arrest.On Saturday, he allegedly told a co-worker that he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” and spoke about a plan involving a Hindu temple in Aurora, a city about 65 kilometres southwest of Palatine.He also told a colleague that Sunday would be “a special day”, according to court documents.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis had been planning an attack for about two years, narrowing his focus to a specific location in recent months. He allegedly researched the target using YouTube and Google Street View.Investigators say the material he shared with a co-worker included an eight-page document titled Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto). According to a court document obtained by the Associated Press, the manifesto described Indian, Jewish and Black people as “subhumans” and outlined a plan to kill as many of them as possible.In the document, Paporakis allegedly described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”. He also portrayed his outward identity as a working college student as a facade concealing his violent intentions, according to the documents.Police believe Paporakis may have attempted to carry out the attack on Sunday, October 11. Surveillance footage showed his car entering the parking lot of a large Hindu temple in Aurora at around 12.25 pm and leaving approximately 13 minutes later. Investigators said he appeared to be alone in the vehicle.The precise intended target has not been officially identified by police and remains under investigation. The Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora subsequently alerted its members to a security threat, according to The New York Times.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis contacted a co-worker later that day and said his gun had jammed. He reportedly said he had left the scene “super fast” without being seen. He also allegedly sent the colleague a video showing the rifle failing to fire and said he wanted to repair it and try again.According to court documents, he told the co-worker that the man he had fired at had been “certainly saved by his God today”. The documents do not establish the identity of the person he allegedly fired at or provide further details about the circumstances.The co-worker contacted police, prompting officers from Palatine and neighbouring Mount Prospect to locate Paporakis. Investigators believed he might attempt to carry out the plan again, and officers arrested him outside his home on Sunday afternoon.A search of Paporakis’ home uncovered an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of ammunition and tactical equipment, police and prosecutors said. Investigators also recovered a tactical vest with body armour, items bearing Nazi symbolism and a gas canister labelled with an anti-South Asian slur.The evidence, along with the alleged manifesto and electronic communications, is being examined as part of the investigation. The FBI’s Chicago Field Office assisted local police in reviewing the material.“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated,” Palatine Police Chief William Nord said, describing the protection of places of worship as a law enforcement priority.Ryan Whalen, the FBI’s Chicago special agent in charge, said the agency worked with local and state authorities to identify and investigate threats driven by extremist ideologies. He credited the rapid response by the Palatine and Mount Prospect police departments with ensuring that the suspect was taken into custody without harm to the community.Paporakis has been charged with making a terrorist threat, a Class X felony, and unlawful possession of a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches, a Class 3 felony. It was not immediately clear whether he had entered a plea or secured legal representation.The case has intensified concerns about hostility towards Indian Americans and other South Asian communities in the United States, particularly as anti-immigration rhetoric and disputes over skilled-worker visas have become increasingly contentious.The FBI does not record crimes against Indian Americans as a separate category. Data on anti-Hindu and anti-Sikh offences therefore offer only a partial picture of the hostility faced by communities whose members often trace their roots to India.Physical attacks and vandalism have also affected Hindu places of worship. In June 2025, between 20 and 30 rounds were reportedly fired at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, while people were inside; no injuries were reported. A separate temple in Santa Clara, California, was vandalised later that summer.Online hostility has been more pronounced. A report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate found that the monthly volume of hateful posts about South Asians on X more than tripled between January 2024 and June 2026.Researchers have linked some of the hostility to disputes over immigration and the H-1B visa programme, which US employers use to hire skilled foreign workers. Indians receive more than 70% of H-1B visas.The ministry of external affairs also said it was “deeply concerned” by the alleged plot, describing its reported anti-Hindu and racist nature as “particularly disturbing”. Official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal called for a thorough investigation, accountability for those responsible and measures to ensure the safety of the Indian community in the US.
Article Summary: Alexandros Paporakis, 19, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches. Police say he had shared a racist manifesto and visited the temple on the day investigators believe he planned to attack. He allegedly described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day’

Article Title: Magnitude 7 earthquake strikes Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula
Article Text:
Preliminary info: M7.0 || 123 km SW of #Vilyuchinsk (Russian Federation)​

A powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck the Kamchatka Peninsula region of Russia on Friday, the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) said, citing seismic data.According to preliminary information shared by EMSC, the earthquake occurred at a depth of 140 km (87 miles), with its epicentre located around 123 km southwest of Vilyuchinsk in Russia’s Far East. The seismic event was recorded at around 3:35 pm local time.The Kamchatka Peninsula, located along the Pacific coast of Russia, is part of the seismically active Pacific Ring of Fire, where tectonic plate movements frequently trigger earthquakes and volcanic activity.The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said there was no tsunami warning, advisory, watch or threat following the earthquake.Further details about the impact of the earthquake, including any reports of damage or casualties, were not immediately available.
Article Summary: Magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes the Kamchatka Peninsula region of Russia on Friday. Quake occurred at a depth of 140 km (87 miles), with epicentre 123 km southwest of Vilyuchinsk. No tsunami warning, advisory, watch or threat following the earthquake.

In a statement, Pannun said the FBI issued a "duty to warn" communication to him on Oct 15, particularly in connection with travel from the United States to Canada to participate in the October 18 Khalistan Referendum in Edmonton, Alberta.The FBI warning follows recent warnings by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) to Pannun allegedly concerning threats to his life and residence in Ontario.In August 2026, the Canadian RCMP had also issued a "Duty to Warn” notifications to three "Khalistan Referendum" organizers: Inderjeet Singh Gosal in Ontario, and Manjinder Singh and Narinder Singh Randhawa in British Columbia.
