Article Title: France protests flare as PM accuses radical left of exploiting unrest ahead of elections
Article Text:
Student protests are sweeping across France as frustrations rise over overcrowded classrooms and poor school facilities

Why the protests are gaining support

France's student protests have intensified ahead of the 2027 presidential election, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu accusing the radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting student anger for electoral gain.According to BBC, thousands of students have taken to the streets over overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school infrastructure and teacher shortages. Trade unions and figures associated with France's Yellow Vest movement are expected to join further demonstrations on Saturday.“Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage,” Lecornu said on Wednesday, accusing the party of encouraging protests while condemning violence.LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has drawn support from demonstrators backing his proposals for a wealth tax, better education and lowering the voting age to 16.The protests come amid mounting pressure on France's public finances and a divided parliament. Economist Anne-Laure Delatte told the BBC that raising taxes could help address the country's debt problem, but warned that such measures would be painful. She also said the European Central Bank could intervene if France's financial difficulties threatened other European economies.The protests have also drawn support from parents who believe demonstrations are necessary to force authorities to address inequality in education.“France likes to speak of égalité, but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit,” three students told the BBC, describing the gap between France’s promise of equality and their experiences.The demonstrations have also revived memories of the May 1968 student movement, which expanded into a major general strike after workers joined the marches.“No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now,” 17-year-old Lola said, reflecting the urgency among young protesters.
Article Summary: Thousands of students have taken to the streets over overcrowded classrooms and poor school facilities. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu accuses the radical- left La France Insoumise of exploiting student anger for electoral gain. Trade unions and figures associated with France's Yellow Vest movement are expected to join further demonstrations on Saturday.

Article Title: Heavenly bamboo was introduced to America in the early 1800s as an ornamental shrub; its red berries can poison birds as the shrub invades forests
Article Text:
Representative Image of a dense growth of heavenly bamboo competing with native plants in a forest landscape (AI-generated image)

What is heavenly bamboo and why is it considered an invasive plant?

How heavenly bamboo spreads into natural areas

Why the red berries can be dangerous to birds

Should heavenly bamboo be planted in gardens?

Introduced to America as an ornamental plant in the early 1800s, heavenly bamboo has become a concern in parts of the country because of its ability to spread into natural areas and its toxic berries. Despite its name, Nandina domestica is not a true bamboo. Native to Asia, this evergreen shrub is grown for its foliage, seasonal flowers and clusters of red berries. However, it can establish itself beyond gardens, spread through vegetative growth and seeds dispersed by birds, and compete with native vegetation. Its berries contain high levels of cyanide and can poison birds and other animals. The shrub’s spread and toxicity have prompted the Missouri Department of Conservation to advise against planting it and recommend removing established plants.Heavenly bamboo, also known as nandina or sacred bamboo, is an evergreen shrub in the barberry family. Native to Asia, it is cultivated for its upright stems, compound leaves and ornamental appearance. The plant typically grows about 3 to 7 feet tall, although its size can vary depending on growing conditions.Its leaves may change colour through the seasons, while its small pinkish-white flowers generally appear in early summer.These are followed by clusters of red berries that can remain on the plant from autumn into spring. The berries contribute to its ornamental appeal but are also a source of concern because of their toxicity. The shrub was introduced to the United States as an ornamental plant in the early 19th century. It has since become established in parts of the country, particularly in the Southeast, where it can grow outside cultivated settings and spread into forests and other natural habitats.Heavenly bamboo can spread through vegetative growth and seed dispersal. Its roots can produce new shoots, while birds that eat the berries can carry seeds away from the parent plant. However, the relative importance of these methods is not settled across the available sources. The US Forest Service’s review of the species reports that seed reproduction may be more common than vegetative reproduction, although the prevalence of each method is not well documented. The Missouri Department of Conservation, meanwhile, highlights the plant’s ability to regrow from its roots. Both pathways can contribute to its spread, and established plants can be difficult to eradicate.Once established outside cultivation, heavenly bamboo can form dense growth that competes with native plants. Its persistent foliage can shade native wildflowers, while dense thickets can limit food sources for wildlife by displacing native vegetation. The shrub’s spread has been documented in Tennessee forests. The Missouri Department of Conservation reports that heavenly bamboo has covered about 10,000 acres of national forest lands in Tennessee alone. Separately, a US Forest Service species review estimates that the plant covered 9,237 acres in Tennessee forests, based on Forest Inventory and Analysis data dated March 15, 2008. The figures refer to different descriptions of the land covered and should not be treated as directly comparable estimates.The Missouri Department of Conservation states that heavenly bamboo’s berries contain high levels of cyanide and can poison wild birds and other animals, including pets. The department documents deaths among cedar waxwings that gorge on the berries, particularly when other types of berries are scarce. The risk does not mean every bird that eats the fruit will be poisoned: the department notes that most birds consume only a few berries at a time and are largely unharmed.Birds also contribute to the shrub’s spread. After eating the fruit, they can deposit undigested seeds far from the parent plant, allowing heavenly bamboo to establish in new locations. This creates a potential double problem: heavy berry consumption can be dangerous to some birds, while seed dispersal can help the non-native shrub spread into natural habitats.The Missouri Department of Conservation advises against planting heavenly bamboo and recommends removing it where it is already growing. The department also notes that no human poisonings have been reported in its account. However, it identifies the plant as toxic and warns of risks to pets and livestock. Removing established plants can require attention to the roots, as regrowth may occur if even a small piece remains in the soil. According to the department, cutting down or burning the above-ground growth can result in resprouting. Control methods may include pulling seedlings, cutting, prescribed burning and herbicide treatments, depending on the situation.Gardeners looking for alternatives can consider native shrubs suited to their local conditions. The Missouri Department of Conservation recommends American beautyberry, Virginia sweet-spire, Carolina allspice, New Jersey tea, wahoo, black chokeberry, fragrant sumac and ninebark. Heavenly bamboo’s history shows how a plant introduced for its appearance can become a management concern outside cultivation. Its ability to spread, the difficulty of controlling established growth and documented bird deaths linked to heavy berry consumption have led the Missouri Department of Conservation to recommend avoiding the plant in favour of suitable native alternatives.
Article Summary: Heavenly bamboo, also known as nandina or sacred bamboo, is an evergreen shrub in the barberry family. Native to Asia, it is cultivated for its upright stems, compound leaves and ornamental appearance. Its leaves may change colour through the seasons, while its small pinkish-white flowers generally appear in early summer. These are followed by clusters of red berries that can remain on the plant from autumn into spring. The berries contribute to its ornamental appeal but are also a source of concern because of their toxicity.

Article Title: 'You'll figure it out': Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver as Republicans, Democrats criticise decision
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia, which Congress had overwhelmingly approved for supporting Ukraine

Lawmakers from both parties criticise Trump

US President Donald Trump has defended his decision to exempt Russia from sweeping sanctions under a new law, calling it a “very good decision” amid criticism from lawmakers across party lines.Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida on Saturday evening, Trump said the implications of his decision were not yet fully understood.“A lot of you don’t know what my decision is yet, but we’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” Trump said, news agency PTI reported.“It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world because we’re really at a world stage,” he added.Trump on Friday signed an executive order exempting Russia from a new sanctions measure passed by Congress last month. The order also granted a waiver from 100% tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India.The exemptions will remain in effect until Trump or the secretary of state, in consultation with the treasury secretary and the US trade representative where appropriate, determines that further action is necessary.Trump’s decision has drawn criticism from Republicans and Democrats who had supported the legislation, known as the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.Republican Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina questioned the decision, saying she would prefer to maintain pressure on Moscow to end the war and bring down energy prices.“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down, because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” she said.Graham had been endorsed by Trump to fill the Senate seat left vacant following the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who had championed the sanctions legislation.Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts accused Trump of disregarding Congress and enabling Putin to continue Russia’s war against Ukraine.Warren urged lawmakers to take action to reverse the decision, adding to the bipartisan criticism of the administration’s approach to sanctions against Moscow.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has defended his decision to exempt Russia from sweeping sanctions under a new law. Trump on Friday signed an executive order exempting Russia from a new sanctions measure passed by Congress last month. The order also granted a waiver from 100% tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India.

Article Title: Dog survives 50 hours alone in Alaska wilderness after avalanche; how rescuers finally found the 4-year-old poodle-husky
Article Text:
LouLou, a four-year-old poodle-husky mix, survived more than 50 hours alone in Alaska’s snowy wilderness after an avalanche.

People

Owner launches search from thousands of miles away

People

People

An Apple AirTag provided crucial clues in the search for LouLou, who went missing after an avalanche near Pepper Peak in Alaska.

How an Apple AirTag helped narrow the search

‘I couldn’t believe what I was seeing’

People

People

After being found on October 12, LouLou was flown to safety. She had a broken toe and a damaged canine tooth but was otherwise doing well.

A rescue made possible by volunteers

A dog named LouLou has been found alive after spending more than 50 hours alone in Alaska’s snowy wilderness, following an avalanche that swept away the two mountaineers she was accompanying. While both men survived the incident but suffered serious injuries, LouLou disappeared into the mountainous terrain, prompting a desperate search that involved more than 20 people, helicopter pilots and a small tracking device that offered a crucial clue.The four-year-old poodle-husky mix was hiking with two experienced mountaineers near Pepper Peak in Alaska’s Chugach State Park on October 10 when an avalanche swept the men approximately 500 feet down a mountain ridge, according toThe men were rescued and taken to hospital, but LouLou could not be found. Her owner, Lauren Padawer, was thousands of miles away when she learnt about the incident and began coordinating efforts to locate her dog.Padawer was overseas celebrating her father’s 80th birthday when news of the avalanche reached her. After learning that both men had survived, she turned her attention to finding LouLou.Unable to reach the mountainous area herself, she contacted local pet rescue groups, hiking organisations, mountaineering groups and people who might be able to help. According to, she reached out to more than 36 individuals as the search gathered momentum.“I just wanted to exhaust every resource I had and only give up [knowing] I did everything I could do,” Padawer told, adding that she was not sleeping much during the ordeal.More than 20 people eventually joined the search, including volunteers on the ground, helicopter pilots, drone operators and a scent-detection dog.The search was complicated by the difficult terrain and changing weather conditions. In the Chugach Mountains, locating a missing animal in deep snow and rugged surroundings was far from straightforward.One important clue was that LouLou was wearing an Apple AirTag. However, the device’s initial location estimate was nearly half a mile off, making it difficult for rescuers to pinpoint her exact position.Padawer explained the challenge in a Facebook post, writing: “On an ordinary map, that might not seem enormous. In the rugged Chugach Mountains, half a mile can mean an entirely different ridge, drainage, or mountainside especially with rapidly shifting and intermittently stormy weather.”Volunteer pilots Amanda Barker and Dave Beckett continued helping with the aerial search. They managed to pick up another signal from LouLou’s AirTag, but worsening weather eventually forced the search to stop for the day.Even from overseas, Padawer continued working to narrow down the possible location. She compared satellite imagery with another mapping application to better understand the terrain and identify the area where the pilots had received the signal.The information helped the team focus its efforts.After approximately 50 hours alone in the wilderness, LouLou was finally spotted on a snowy mountainside on October 12. The helicopter landed, and rescuers approached her on foot before flying her to safety.For Padawer, the moment she learnt that LouLou had been found was difficult to comprehend.“I was shocked!” she told. “I couldn’t believe what I was seeing. It was too good to be true. I cried.”LouLou was subsequently examined and found to have suffered relatively minor injuries, including a broken toe and a damaged canine tooth. Otherwise, she was doing well and had returned home to rest.“She’s amazing, she appears to have broken a toe and a canine tooth. She’s enjoying the couch and naps. Otherwise back to normal.”The owner also believed LouLou’s familiarity with outdoor environments may have helped her endure the ordeal. The dog regularly accompanied her owner on backcountry skiing trips and was accustomed to spending time on mountain trails.“She’s a seasoned backcountry skier companion dog and is very good at following the trail back,” Padawer toldwhile describing LouLou’s temperament and love for the outdoors.She also pointed to the dog’s thick coat as a possible advantage in the cold conditions. “I think she’s just built for cold… she’s got a soft downy undercoat and thick curly guard hairs,” she said.While LouLou’s survival after more than two days alone in the mountains was remarkable, Padawer credited the people who kept searching despite the difficult conditions.She particularly praised pilots Barker and Beckett for helping locate and retrieve the dog.“Their generosity, skill, and determination turned a desperate search into an extraordinary homecoming,” Padawer wrote on Facebook.For the owner, the reunion brought an end to a frightening wait that had unfolded across thousands of miles. For the rescue team, it was the result of sustained coordination, aerial searches and the use of whatever clues were available.And LouLou, after an ordeal that left her with a broken toe and a damaged tooth, was back home doing what her owner said she was enjoying most: resting on the couch and taking naps.
Article Summary: LouLou, a four-year-old poodle-husky mix, survived more than 50 hours alone in Alaska’s snowy wilderness after an avalanche. She was hiking with two experienced mountaineers near Pepper Peak on October 10 when an avalanche swept the men approximately 500 feet down a mountain ridge. While both men survived the incident but suffered serious injuries, LouLou disappeared into the mountainous terrain. A desperate search involved more than 20 people, helicopter pilots and a small tracking device that offered crucial clues.

Article Title: Karmelo Anthony's first fundraiser raised nearly $634,000; family now seeks another $250,000 for murder appeal as questions remain over earlier funds
Article Text:
Karmelo Anthony(Left) and Austin Metcalf, who was stabbed to death by Anthony(Right). Image Credit: Texas Department of Criminal Justice/FOX News

Why is Karmelo Anthony's family seeking another $250,000

The earlier fundraiser covered much more than legal fees

Anthony's claim of financial hardship faces scrutiny

Online criticism grows over the fresh fundraising request

The appeal moves forward as questions remain

Karmelo Anthony’s family has launched a new fundraiser seeking $250,000 to pay for his appeal after an earlier campaign raised nearly $634,000. The fresh fundraising effort has renewed questions about how the previous donations were spent, particularly after Anthony said he could not afford a lawyer to challenge his murder conviction. According to Fox News, the new campaign is structured differently, with donations intended to go directly into an attorney’s trust account. However, the family’s latest appeal has also drawn criticism online.The new fundraising campaign was announced at a news conference in Dallas, Texas, following a judge’s rejection of Anthony’s request for a new trial. The 19-year-old was sentenced to 35 years in prison in June 2026 after a jury convicted him of murdering 17-year-old Austin Metcalf during a high school track meet in Frisco, Texas, in April 2025.According to Fox News, the family and its supporters, including attorney Russell Wilson, outlined plans to challenge the conviction through the appeals process. The new campaign aims to raise $250,000 to cover the costs associated with that legal challenge.The money will reportedly be used for legal expenses, including court filings, transcripts, investigators and expert witnesses. Unlike the earlier campaign, the new arrangement places the donations in a trust account administered by Wilson, rather than allowing the family to receive or control the funds directly.The first campaign, titled ‘Help Karmelo Official Fund,’ was launched on GiveSendGo on 15 April 2025, less than 2 weeks after the fatal stabbing. Organised by Anthony’s mother, Kala Hayes, it initially set a target of nearly $1.4 million and eventually collected just under $634,000.As reported by Fox News, the campaign was not intended to cover legal expenses alone. Its stated purpose also included helping the family relocate because of safety concerns, as well as paying for basic living expenses, transport, counselling and security measures.The family faced threats and unwanted attention as the case attracted national interest. The broader purpose of the fundraiser was presented as a way to help them manage the consequences of the case alongside the legal proceedings.GiveSendGo later confirmed that the donations had been distributed over the preceding year for lawful purposes, including legal defence and family relocation. The platform said the campaign had been closed because its stated purpose had been completed.But the fundraiser's removal following Anthony's conviction did not end questions about the money. Instead, the family's subsequent claim that it needed further financial assistance for his appeal brought the earlier donations back into public discussion.The question of legal expenses became more prominent after Anthony filed a notice of appeal following his conviction. Anthony's court filing described him as unable to afford a lawyer to represent him during the appeal and sought recognition of his financial hardship.The timing attracted attention because hundreds of thousands of dollars had already been raised in his name. Critics questioned why another fundraiser was necessary when the original campaign had collected such a substantial sum.The family’s spokesperson, civil rights activist Dominique Alexander, was questioned about the earlier donations during the news conference announcing the new campaign. Fox News reported that Alexander rejected allegations that the family had used the money improperly but did not provide a detailed breakdown of the previous fund's expenditure.He also declined to explain the family's fees or confirm whether any money from the earlier campaign remained available.The distinction between the two campaigns is important. The original fundraiser explicitly allowed donations to support several family needs, whereas the new campaign says the money will be restricted to legal expenses associated with the appeal.The new campaign has also prompted a wave of negative reactions on social media. The criticism reflects a broader dispute over how crowdfunding campaigns should communicate their purpose, particularly when donations are collected for someone facing a serious criminal conviction.However, online reactions do not establish that the family misused donations. The earlier campaign's stated terms allowed spending on relocation and living costs as well as legal defence. GiveSendGo has also said the money was distributed for lawful purposes consistent with the campaign's stated objectives.The latest fundraising effort marks another stage in Anthony's legal battle, with the new money intended to support his challenge to the murder conviction. His legal team has indicated that the appeal will involve further court filings and may require investigators and expert witnesses.According to Fox News, Anthony maintains that he cannot afford to hire a lawyer for the appeal, despite the substantial sum previously raised on his behalf. His family's supporters argue that challenging the conviction requires further legal work, while critics want clearer answers about the earlier donations.
Article Summary: Karmelo Anthony’s family has launched a new fundraiser seeking $250,000 to pay for his appeal after an earlier campaign raised nearly $634,000. The money will reportedly be used for legal expenses, including court filings, transcripts, investigators and expert witnesses. The fresh fundraising effort has renewed questions about how the previous donations were spent, particularly after Anthony said he could not afford a lawyer to challenge his murder conviction. The new campaign has also prompted a wave of negative reactions on social media.

Article Title: A California farm earned about $100 per acre a year from dry-farmed wheat; after Alan Changala leased 300 acres for solar at $1,000 per acre, the same land began paying roughly 10 times the crop incom
Article Text:
Representative image

Dry farming left little margin

Solar became the better crop

Water shortages changed the math

Solar brings income but few jobs

A difficult trade-off for the Valley

On the Changala family farm in Tulare County, California, a dirt road and a barbed-wire fence separate two very different ways of using the same land. On one side, wheat grows with little irrigation. On the other, rows of solar panels turn sunlight into electricity for thousands of Southern California homes. For Alan Changala, the choice was not sentimental. The solar lease paid about ten times what the dry-farmed wheat could earn.Changala leased 300 acres of his father’s 1,400-acre farm to solar developers at $1,000 per acre, while the wheat operation generated roughly $100 per acre annually, reported The Sacramento Bee. The deal, negotiated at the family kitchen table in 2014, became part of a wider shift across California’s San Joaquin Valley, where farmers facing water shortages and rising costs are looking to solar as a way to keep their businesses viable. Read more about it here, as reported by The Sacramento Bee:The Changala farm had water available from wells and an irrigation canal, but using it was expensive. Instead, Alan Changala said nearly the entire property was dry-farmed, relying on rainfall rather than irrigation.That approach allowed wheat to be planted on about half the farm every other year, using a rotation system that preserved soil moisture.The economics were modest. Changala told The Sacramento Bee that the wheat business worked out to an annual income of about $100 per acre. In a region where water has become both scarce and costly, that limited return made it difficult to justify expanding irrigation or relying entirely on traditional crops.When solar developers began showing interest in the property, Changala saw an opportunity rather than a betrayal of his farming roots. He described himself as “a farmer, through and through,” but acknowledged that the lease was simply more profitable than continuing to farm every acre.The lease covered 300 acres and paid $1,000 per acre, giving the family an income roughly ten times higher than the wheat operation. Changala said the arrangement did not take much persuasion, even though he negotiated carefully. Hal Dittmer of Sacramento renewable-energy developer Wellhead Electric personally negotiated the deal with the Changala family in 2014, as per the report.Construction took place in 2015 and 2016. The completed project, technically made up of two facilities called Nicolis and Tropico, has a generating capacity of 34 megawatts and produces enough electricity to power about 9,000 homes in Southern California Edison’s service area. But Changala’s father, Si Changala, was less comfortable with the change. Still, he accepted the reality of the decision, saying farmers had to “go with the times. ”The shift toward solar is closely tied to California’s water crisis. The state’s Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, known as SGMA, requires farmers to gradually reduce groundwater pumping in areas where aquifers have been depleted by decades of overuse. In the San Joaquin Valley, that could mean retiring large amounts of farmland over the next two decades.The Public Policy Institute of California predicted that at least 535,000 acres of Valley farmland could be permanently retired over 20 years as farmers cut water use. The institute also estimated that about 50,000 of those idled acres could be converted to solar farms.For farmers like Changala, solar offers a way to earn steady income from land that may no longer be practical to farm. He was even negotiating to lease another 400 acres for a second solar facility, a move that would further reduce the footprint of the family’s wheat operation.The financial benefits for individual landowners are clear, but the broader economic effects are more complicated. Solar farms create substantial employment during construction, but once the panels are operating, they require relatively few permanent workers. On the Changala property, workers arrived in school buses during installation, but the completed site now depends mainly on occasional maintenance visits and remote operations based in Southern California.Local officials worry that this lack of permanent employment weakens the economic base of rural communities. In Kern County, where thousands of acres have already been converted to solar, planning director Lorelei Oviatt said land removed from farming “doesn’t pay for libraries,” pointing to the county’s need for jobs, services and quality of life for its 900,000 residents.There are also concerns about tax revenue. California allowed solar project owners to avoid property taxes on the value of installed panels, meaning many facilities were taxed as though the land remained agricultural. Critics said the break, which was set to run until 2025, shifted costs away from a mature industry and onto counties.California still needs solar power. Utilities in the state received one-third of their electricity from renewable sources at the time, and state law required that share to rise to 60 percent by 2030 and 100 percent by 2045. The San Joaquin Valley, with its abundant sunlight and large tracts of land, could play a major role in meeting those targets.But converting farmland to solar is not a simple solution. Community leaders worry about unplanned patches of retired land, dust, weeds and air-quality problems. Some farm groups are working with environmental organisations to create conservation easements that would pay farmers to restore land as wildlife habitat rather than leave it idle or cover it with panels.For the Changala family, however, the decision came down to survival. Wheat still grows on one side of the fence, but solar panels now provide a far stronger financial foundation on the other. As Alan Changala put it, “We’re still farming the sun.”
Article Summary: The Changala family in Tulare County, California, leased 300 acres of their 1,400-acre farm to solar developers at $1,000 per acre. The solar lease paid about ten times what the dry-farmed wheat could earn. The deal, negotiated at the family kitchen table in 2014, became part of a wider shift across California’s San Joaquin Valley.

Article Title: In 1968, Cassandra Henderson graduated from a North Carolina school; nearly 60 years later, she moved back into the same building after it was restored from 20 years of vacancy into 53 senior apartmen
Article Text:
In 1968, Cassandra Henderson graduated from a North Carolina school; 58 years later, she returned to its restored building, now 53 senior apartments (Image Credit: The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition)

From school corridors to affordable homes

A former school gets a second life

What the 53 apartments offer

Addressing North Carolina's senior housing shortage

How the restoration was financed

Nearly six decades after graduating from Dillard Junior High School in Yanceyville, North Carolina, Cassandra Henderson has returned to the same building, this time as a resident of its newly restored senior apartments. The former school, which closed in 2002 and remained vacant for more than 20 years, has been transformed into 53 affordable homes for older adults. According to NC Newsline, which reported on the redevelopment, the project combines historic preservation with an effort to address the shortage of affordable housing for seniors. The development has also received national recognition from the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition.Henderson graduated from the school in 1968 and later spent years living in Richmond, Virginia. When she wanted to return to Yanceyville to be closer to family and friends, finding suitable housing became an obstacle. Her sister encouraged her to move home, but Henderson recalled telling her there was nowhere for her to live. The redevelopment changed that. Henderson moved into the Dillard School Apartments in August 2026, returning to the entrance where she once arrived by school bus.In an interview with NC Newsline, she recalled the school’s hallways, metal lockers and auditorium, describing her years there as some of her happiest.She also expressed relief that the building had been preserved and given a new purpose. Her experience illustrates how converting an unused historic property into housing can help older residents remain connected to the communities where they grew up.The building originally opened as the Caswell County Training School between 1949 and 1951. It was the first school in Caswell County to offer 11 grades to Black students. Following desegregation in 1969, it was renamed Dillard Junior High School in honour of Nicholas Longworth Dillard, a longtime principal.The school closed in 2002 and was subsequently listed on the National Register of Historic Places. However, it remained unused for more than two decades, with broken windows, a deteriorating gymnasium roof and interiors exposed to the elements.Alex Walker, a representative of the project's developer, DreamKey Partners, told NC Newsline that the conversion offered an opportunity to preserve the historic building while putting it back into productive use. Rather than demolishing the property, the redevelopment retained its historic character and adapted the former educational spaces for residential use.The completed Dillard School Senior Apartments development contains 53 affordable homes for residents aged 62 and older. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, the property comprises seven studio apartments and 46 one-bedroom units, with rents restricted to households earning no more than 50% of the area median income. Residents pay up to 30% of their income towards rent, with federal housing assistance covering the remaining eligible costs. The development is intended for older adults who can live independently rather than those requiring assisted-living services.The property also includes elevators, accessible features, a community centre with computer and fitness facilities, communal laundry, tenant storage and community gardens. Outdoor amenities include pickleball and shuffleboard courts, while on-site management helps coordinate services for residents.These facilities are intended to make the apartments practical for older adults while providing opportunities for recreation and social interaction.The redevelopment comes as affordable housing remains difficult to find for many older North Carolinians living on fixed incomes. According to figures cited by NC Newsline, approximately 42% of renters and 20% of homeowners in Caswell County spend more than 30% of their gross monthly income on housing. Across North Carolina, the estimated shortage of affordable rental homes for extremely low-income households stands at 215,000.Charity James, property manager at Dillard School Apartments, told NC Newsline that the community has few affordable housing developments, particularly those designed for seniors. She said demand exceeded the number of available apartments when leasing began, resulting in long waiting lists. The project cannot resolve the wider housing shortage on its own, but it provides an example of how unused public-serving buildings can be adapted to meet local housing needs.The project combined several funding sources, including the US Department of Housing and Urban Development's Section 202 programme and state and federal historic tax credits. Walker told NC Newsline that combining these financing mechanisms, particularly HUD support, made it possible to restore the property and provide affordable homes. The development received the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition's 2026 Recognition of Housing Tax Credit Excellence award in the rural housing category. Emily Cadik, the coalition's chief executive, said the winning projects had made lasting contributions to their communities by providing families with affordable places to live.For Henderson, however, the redevelopment's importance is personal. She has returned not simply to her hometown but to a building that holds memories of her school years. In an interview with NC Newsline, she described being back as a source of renewed energy and said she felt she was where she belonged. The former school now serves a different generation, preserving a piece of local history while giving older residents an opportunity to remain close to home.
Article Summary: Cassandra Henderson graduated from Dillard Junior High School in Yanceyville, North Carolina, in 1968. The former school closed in 2002 and remained vacant for more than 20 years. It has now been transformed into 53 affordable homes for older adults. The development has received national recognition from the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition.

Article Title: How a Brooklyn crypto cop took down a global scam network
Article Text:
As crypto use has become more widespread, the global crypto fraud economy has exploded in size

By the time Alona Katz hurried home from her office in downtown Brooklyn late on Oct 6, the trap was already set. After months of planning, the chief of Brooklyn’s crypto fraud unit was about to orchestrate one of the most sweeping international crackdowns a local prosecutor’s office had ever attempted. The operation, which took place across three time zones, was the culmination of a chase Katz had begun almost as soon as she was appointed chief of Brooklyn District Attorney’s Virtual Currency Unit three years ago.At 2am, dozens of servers that Katz’s team had targeted started going down. She would get no sleep that night.As crypto use has become more widespread, the global crypto fraud economy has exploded in size. In 2025, reported US losses from cryptocurrency fraud reached $11.4 billion, roughly triple from three years earlier, according to the FBI.Before the Brooklyn DA opened the VCU office, victims who sought help from the New York Police Dept were often told to go elsewhere because the NYPD didn’t understand the scams, Eric Gonzalez, the Brooklyn District Attorney, said in an interview.Frustrated as the number of fraud victims soared, Gonzalez decided to set up a special unit to handle it, and hired Katz in 2023 from the Manhattan DA’s cybercrime and identity-theft bureau.Katz, in her 40s, doesn’t have a background in computer programming. She reads poetry, and most of her family are artists.“I was the black sheep for going to law school,” she said.Her phone lit up as soon as she started her new job. Katz soon noticed a pattern in the calls coming into her office. Many victims were from Brighton Beach and Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn communities heavily populated by Russian and Ukrainian immigrants. The scammers, who typically conversed in Russian, identified themselves as fellow immigrants who’d found success trading in the US.The cons were simple. Scammers contacted victims on social networks and persuaded them to invest a few hundred dollars in crypto trades. Small withdrawals were allowed but when victims tried to cash out, they were charged costly fees or ghosted.Katz spent most working hours watching Bitcoin and Tether tokens move between digital wallets, learning the contours of vast underground international fraud networks and how to stop them. Crypto’s transparency aids investigators because transactions are recorded on a public ledger, or blockchain, allowing those with suitable software to follow money between wallets. Over months, Katz and her team identified websites the scammers had set up, and moved to shut them down.Patterns they unearthed include similar branding by these sites, which exposed a cyber infrastructure located in Eastern Europe, including Ukraine. But site seizures proved temporary. Seeking a lasting impact, Katz’s team has developed undisclosed methods to identify servers underpinning the scams.Bloomberg
Article Summary: In 2025, reported US losses from cryptocurrency fraud reached $11.4 billion, roughly triple from three years earlier, according to the FBI. Scammers contacted victims on social networks and persuaded them to invest a few hundred dollars in crypto trades. Many victims were from Brighton Beach and Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn communities heavily populated by Russian and Ukrainian immigrants.

Article Title: Anthropic pitches own AI Safety Bill
Article Text:
The bill would mandate that AI makers must test their models and share findings with the public

Anthropic has presented its own draft bill to US lawmakers with a plan for regulating artificial intelligence safety and security, in a moment of heightened concern about the potential risks of the rapidly advancing technology.The proposal suggests govt could block the release of an AI model if it’s determined to imminently risk killing or injuring over 50 people or causing more than $1billion in damage, according to Politico, which first reported on the bill. The threat must be a result of the model creating or releasing a biological weapon, the AI going beyond human control, or a cyberattack, Politico reported.“This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” a company spokesperson said. The bill would mandate that AI makers must test their models and share findings with the public; it also would require AI companies to allow independent evaluators to routinely review models, the spokesperson said.“Our proposal also grants the federal govt the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models,” the spokesperson said. “These are sensible policies we believe Congress should act on.”Bloomberg
Article Summary: Proposal suggests govt could block the release of an AI model if it’s determined to imminently risk killing or injuring over 50 people or causing more than $1billion in damage. The threat must be a result of the model creating or releasing a biological weapon, the AI going beyond human control, or a cyberattack.

Article Title: US Congressman’s Krishnamoorthi’s office receives suspicious package as FBI probes nationwide mail threats
Article Text:
Indian-origin US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi

Federal agencies investigate nationwide mailings

More lawmakers report suspicious deliveries

US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi ’s district office in Schaumburg, Illinois, received a suspicious package containing unknown substances, prompting a response from local emergency services and federal law enforcement, as investigators probe similar mailings targeting congressional offices and election officials across the United States.Krishnamoorthi confirmed the incident in a post on X on Saturday, saying the package was safely removed. The incident comes amid a nationwide investigation into suspicious letters and packages sent to lawmakers and election officials, with the FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service leading the probe."Yesterday, my district office received a suspicious package similar to those sent to multiple congressional offices across the country," Krishnamoorthi said.The congressman thanked the emergency responders and law enforcement agencies involved in the operation."I am grateful for the Schaumburg Fire Department, the Postal Inspector, Capitol Police, and federal law enforcement for their swift response in safely removing the package and its substances," he stated.Reflecting on the incident, he added, "It’s been a long week."The incident comes as federal investigators examine a series of suspicious letters sent to state election officials and congressional offices across the country, several of which reportedly contained unidentified substances, CBS News reported.The investigation is being conducted jointly by the FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), which has confirmed that authorities are tracking suspicious mailings across multiple jurisdictions.According to CBS News, Brendan Donahue, deputy chief inspector at the USPIS, said investigators had discovered unknown substances in some envelopes. The mailings were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including "secretary of state offices and the related election offices."The reported targets include lawmakers from both major political parties. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's office was among the congressional locations identified in the investigation, while at least two Senate Republicans also received letters, CBS News reported.Amid the security concerns, the Senate Sergeant at Arms issued a formal notice to Capitol Hill staff informing them of the ongoing multi-agency investigation.Democratic Representative Bobby Scott also said federal authorities had intercepted a package containing an unknown, potentially hazardous substance addressed to his district office.Scott said federal agents contacted his staff to inform them that the package had been seized before it reached its destination."The FBI contacted my office earlier today to report that it had intercepted mail containing a suspicious substance addressed to my district office, like others reported around the country," Scott wrote in a post on X.He thanked law enforcement agencies for their intervention and condemned attempts to intimidate elected representatives and their staff."I am grateful to law enforcement for their efforts to keep my staff safe," Scott stated. "Threats and attempts at intimidation are unacceptable and must not be tolerated."CBS News cited the USPIS deputy chief inspector as saying that investigators were working to identify those responsible for the mailings, with authorities intercepting some packages before delivery.The incidents come about three weeks before the US midterm elections. Federal authorities had also investigated widespread suspicious letter campaigns in the run-up to the 2024 elections.
Article Summary: US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi's district office in Schaumburg, Illinois, received a suspicious package. The package contained unknown substances, prompting a response from local emergency services and federal law enforcement. The incident comes amid a nationwide investigation into suspicious letters and packages sent to lawmakers and election officials.

Article Title: San Diego is weighing a $4.2 billion redevelopment of 48.5 city-owned acres with 4,254 homes, a $526.4 million arena and $460.3 million in infrastructure and park improvements
Article Text:
San Diego is weighing a $4.2 billion redevelopment of 48.5 city-owned acres with 4,254 homes, a $526.4 million arena and $460.3 million in infrastructure and park improvements (Image Credit: City of San Diego)

What the $4.2 billion redevelopment includes

A new arena and hundreds of millions for infrastructure

Why the city is prioritising housing and public amenities

What happens next

San Diego is advancing a proposed $4.2 billion redevelopment of 48.5 acres of city-owned land around the Pechanga Arena, with plans for thousands of homes, a new entertainment venue and major public infrastructure improvements. According to the City of San Diego’s official Midway Rising project page, the proposal includes 4,254 housing units, a 16,000-seat arena and new parks and public spaces in the Midway District. On October 16, 2026, the City Council’s Land Use and Housing Committee unanimously voted to advance the proposal, bringing the long-delayed project closer to consideration by the full City Council.The Midway Rising proposal aims to transform the existing Sports Arena property into a mixed-use neighbourhood combining residential buildings, entertainment, retail, parks and improved streets. The development team is expected to finance the estimated $4.2 billion project, which would replace the ageing arena and parking-dominated site with a more integrated urban district. The housing component includes 2,000 affordable homes and 2,254 market-rate units. The affordable housing allocation includes at least 200 permanent supportive housing units intended to serve people who need additional support to maintain stable housing.The plan also proposes up to 130,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, creating room for shops, dining and other businesses. The wider development is designed to make the area more walkable, improve connections to public transport and provide more public spaces for residents and visitors. The project is being developed by Midway Rising, a consortium that includes Zephyr, The Kroenke Group, Legends and Chelsea Investment Corporation.A central feature of the proposal is a new multipurpose arena costing an estimated $526.4 million. Designed to accommodate 16,000 people, the venue would replace the existing Pechanga Arena as the area's main entertainment destination. The development also includes $460.3 million in infrastructure and public improvements. These are expected to cover street upgrades, pedestrian-friendly routes, parking facilities, parks and other improvements in and around the site. The plan provides approximately 14.5 acres of combined park and public space, offering recreational areas alongside the new housing and commercial development.Construction would take place in phases. The first phase is expected to deliver the new arena alongside affordable and market-rate housing. The existing arena would continue operating until its replacement is ready to open, allowing scheduled events to continue during the transition. The overall development is expected to take years, with the city’s Independent Budget Analyst estimating that full buildout could take about 20 years, although the developer has projected a shorter construction period of around 10 to 15 years.The proposal reflects a financial trade-off for San Diego. Instead of prioritising immediate rental income from its land, the city is seeking substantial private investment in affordable housing, entertainment facilities and infrastructure. Under the proposed arrangement, the developer would make investments upfront, while the city would receive revenue through arena ticket fees and rent from market-rate housing and retail as different phases are completed. The timing and amount of those payments would depend on construction progress and the project's financial performance.The city has also proposed an Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District to help fund infrastructure costs. Under this arrangement, increases in property tax revenue above an established baseline could be used to reimburse eligible development infrastructure expenses over time. The city’s Independent Budget Analyst estimates that the developer could be reimbursed for up to $378 million of its infrastructure spending through the proposed financing district. The arrangement means the public benefits would be delivered before the city receives the full financial returns. The proposed agreement therefore includes provisions for oversight as the project progresses.The project has faced years of delays and legal challenges, including disputes concerning coastal building-height restrictions. In September 2026, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation intended to help clear the way for the redevelopment while retaining environmental review requirements. The October 16 committee vote marks another important step, but it does not constitute final approval by the full City Council. The proposed development agreements and related financing arrangements must still move through the remaining approval process before construction can begin.If approved, Midway Rising would reshape a major city-owned property into a residential and entertainment district, with thousands of homes and significant public improvements. Its eventual impact will depend on whether the developer delivers the promised housing, infrastructure and public spaces while managing the financial and construction challenges of a multibillion-dollar project.
Article Summary: San Diego is weighing a $4.2 billion redevelopment of 48.5 city-owned acres with 4,254 homes, a $526.4 million arena and $460.3 million in infrastructure and park improvements. On October 16, 2026, the City Council’s Land Use and Housing Committee unanimously voted to advance the proposal, bringing the long-delayed project closer to consideration by the full City Council.

Article Title: Strong 6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan
Article Text:
6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan

More details awaited

An earthquake measuring 6.0 in magnitude struck southern Pakistan near Khuzdar, Balochistan on Saturday, around 95 km south of Sūrāb, according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC).The German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) said the earthquake struck at a depth of 10 km (6 miles).
Article Summary: An earthquake measuring 6.0 in magnitude struck southern Pakistan near Khuzdar, Balochistan on Saturday. The German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) said the earthquake struck at a depth of 10 km (6 miles)

Article Title: Imran Khan facing Nawaz, Benazir-style exile deal? Pakistan opposition leader's big claim
Article Text:
Imran Khan

What happened in Nawaz Sharif, Benazir Bhutto's exile cases?

Achakzai demands access to prisoners, empowered parliament

Opposition challenges governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Pakistan opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai has claimed that jailed former prime minister Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to arrangements that led former premiers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto into exile, according to a report by Dawn published on Saturday.Achakzai, chairman of the Pakhtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PkMAP) and leader of the opposition in Pakistan's National Assembly, made the claim at a news conference at the Peshawar high court on Friday. He alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) were involved in a similar political arrangement.“The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Achakzai said, according to Dawn.The claim comes amid political tensions surrounding Imran Khan, founder of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), who remains in prison, and opposition allegations over restrictions on political activity and the functioning of elected institutions.Achakzai was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. He said opposition parties were in contact and that a multi-party conference would be convened soon.He also said resigning from the assemblies remained an option, adding that the opposition had submitted its demands in response to an offer of negotiations.Achakzai's remarks referred to the circumstances in which Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, two of Pakistan's most prominent former prime ministers, spent periods outside the country following political upheavals, Dawnreported.Sharif was ousted and imprisoned after a military coup led by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf. He left Pakistan in 2000 under a deal negotiated with the involvement of Saudi and Lebanese leaders.Bhutto, meanwhile, went into self-imposed exile after her Pakistan Peoples Party lost the 1997 general elections, following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leghari. Her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, was imprisoned on corruption charges and was released in 2004.Achakzai's comparison suggests that he believes a similar arrangement could be pursued in Khan's case. However, his remarks, as reported by Dawn, did not establish that an exile agreement involving the PTI founder had been reached.During the news conference, Achakzai criticised restrictions on prisoners' access to meetings and called for changes to what he described as a "wrong amendment". He also demanded that parliament be empowered and an independent commission be established to ensure transparent elections.“Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, according to Dawn.He argued that political disputes could not be resolved without strengthening parliament. He also expressed concern over the whereabouts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's chief minister and other lawmakers, demanding that the authorities disclose the chief minister's location.“We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived.Mengal, who accompanied Achakzai, criticised the government's actions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and questioned the imposition of governor's rule on grounds of terrorism. He also alleged that elected representatives had been displaced and questioned the legitimacy of the political system.Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, also criticised the situation, saying: “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” according to Dawn.Separately, TTAP leaders approached the Peshawar High Court on Friday, challenging the proclamation of emergency and the imposition of governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to Dawn, the petitioners asked the court to declare the October 11 proclamation, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of Pakistan's Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority. They argued that the constitutional conditions required for imposing the measures had not been met or that the government had exceeded its powers.The petition also challenged the purported transfer of the provincial assembly's legislative powers to parliament, the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet, and the establishment of the proposed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat.The petitioners sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications linked to the proclamation, including the deployment of armed forces to the extent that it allegedly violated constitutional requirements.They also requested interim relief to prevent the displacement of elected institutions and restrictions on elected representatives while the court considers the case.The legal challenge adds to the opposition's broader campaign against federal intervention in the province, as Achakzai seeks to bring opposition parties together over constitutional issues, political rights and negotiations with the government.
Article Summary: Mahmood Khan Achakzai claims Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to those that led Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto into exile. He claims the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) are involved in a similar political arrangement. The opposition leader made the claim at a news conference at the Peshawar high court on Friday.

Article Title: Pakistan to chair IMF, World Bank boards in 2027; first time in over 70 years
Article Text:
The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok (Photo: AP).

Pakistan will take over the chairmanship of the boards of governors of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in 2027, returning to the position for the first time since 1953, the country’s ministry of economic affairs said on Friday.The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, where Pakistan’s minister for economic affairs Ahad Khan Cheema, who also serves as the country’s governor to the World Bank, was formally designated as the incoming chair, PTI reported.Describing the appointment as a “historic milestone”, the ministry said the role would allow Pakistan to participate in shaping global economic and development discussions and encourage constructive engagement among member countries.The annual meetings, scheduled from October 12 to 18, have brought together more than 15,000 participants representing 191 countries.The appointment comes as Pakistan continues to rely on financial assistance from the IMF through two programmes: a USD 7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a USD 1.4 billion Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).While the EFF is aimed at meeting the country’s balance-of-payments needs and supporting economic reforms, the RSF provides longer-term funding to help Pakistan tackle climate-related risks and improve its resilience.Pakistan could receive a further USD 1.2 billion from the IMF, subject to approval by the fund’s Executive Board. The anticipated disbursement follows an agreement reached between IMF staff and Pakistani authorities on the latest reviews of both programmes.
Article Summary: Pakistan will take over the chairmanship of the boards of governors of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in 2027. The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok. Pakistan continues to rely on financial assistance from the IMF through two programmes.

Article Title: Pakistan ranks lowest in South Asia on hunger index amid rising food prices
Article Text:
Pakistan's 2026 Global Hunger Index standings reveal an alarming crisis, showcasing the worst performance in South Asia amid ongoing economic challenges. (Pic Credit: ANI)

Economic crisis and food inflation worsen Pakistan’s hunger situation

Hunger reduction stalls across South Asia

Extreme weather threatens regional food production

Millions across South Asia continue to face undernourishment

Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI), reflecting mounting food insecurity driven by economic instability, rising food prices, climate-related disasters and international conflicts, according to a report by Dawn.Titled “No Security Without Food Security”, the report was jointly prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas.According to the news agency ANI, the findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated, while Pakistan and Afghanistan have experienced a deterioration in conditions since 2018.Pakistan’s economic challenges and persistent food inflation have eroded household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for families to access sufficient and nutritious food.The report noted that Pakistan’s undernourishment indicator had deteriorated from a low level in 2018 to a medium level. Meanwhile, child wasting has approached the threshold associated with the high category, underscoring continuing concerns over child nutrition.South Asia recorded an overall global hunger index score of 23.5, placing the region in the serious category. While the score represents an improvement from 37.5 in 2000, the report suggests that much of the progress was achieved before 2018.Over the past two decades, Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved out of the alarming hunger category. However, persistent levels of child malnutrition continue to pose a significant challenge in both countries.Child stunting has continued to decline in Pakistan, while Afghanistan has recorded a slight increase in the indicator since 2018.Child mortality rates have improved in both countries, falling from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels in the latest assessment.The report also drew attention to the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural production and food security across South Asia.Heavy rainfall and flooding damaged crops in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh. In Afghanistan, inadequate rainfall and unusually high temperatures disrupted the cereal-growing season in 2026.These climate-related pressures could further aggravate food shortages and prolong acute food insecurity across the region, according to Dawn.Estimates from the food and agriculture organisation (FAO) indicate that approximately 218 million people across South Asia, including Iran, experienced undernourishment between 2023 and 2025.This represents roughly one-third of the global population affected by undernourishment during the period, highlighting the scale of the region’s food security challenge.The findings underscore the need for sustained efforts to address economic vulnerabilities, improve access to nutritious food and strengthen agricultural resilience against climate-related shocks.
Article Summary: Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI) The report was prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas. The findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated.

Article Title: 33 children, teacher killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan’s Peshawar
Article Text:
18 killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan's Peshawar

At least 33 students and a teacher were killed after the roof of a school collapsed in Pakistan 's Peshawar city on Thursday.Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident, officials said.Peshawar Capital City Police chief Mian Saeed said the incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area, as cited by PTI.Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Muhammad Asim said an emergency had been declared at the facility to treat the injured.All the children killed in the incident were aged 13 or younger, Asim said. Rescue officials said 25 injured children had been taken to medical facilities.Rescue teams were clearing the debris and searching for children and school staff who might still be trapped beneath the collapsed structure.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.Building and roof collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and the use of substandard construction materials.In July, three girls aged between three and 13 were killed when part of the outer wall of a government primary school near Umerkot collapsed, burying them under the debris, as cited by Dawn.That same month, a child was killed and at least five others were injured when the roof of an under-construction private school building collapsed in Lahore’s Baghbanpura neighbourhood.In June, 14 children died after the roof of a private tuition centre collapsed in Lahore’s Kahna area. Less than two months earlier, four children were killed and 20 people injured when a classroom roof collapsed at a private school in Dera Ghazi Khan.
Article Summary: Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident. The incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.

Article Title: Pakistan regulator warns TV channels against live coverage of blasts and terror attacks
Article Text:
The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight.

Channels told to air only verified information

Legal action for violations

Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks, cautioning that violations could lead to legal action.The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday, reminding broadcasters of restrictions first introduced on February 20, 2023. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting, rebroadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.The directive comes as emergency rule has been imposed in the north-western province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, renewing debate over how the media should report security incidents while ensuring that the public receives timely and reliable information.PEMRA has instructed broadcasters to air only “verified information warranted by the relevant government departments or law enforcement agencies”.The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight and the effective use of broadcast delays to prevent the immediate transmission of sensitive footage during security incidents.It directed television channels to establish independent editorial boards in line with applicable laws and relevant court judgments.The notification referred to the Supreme Court's judgment in Suo Motu Case No. 28 of 2018 and an Islamabad High Court order dated September 5, 2022, both concerning the prescribed procedure for broadcast delays.PEMRA warned that channels violating the directive could face legal proceedings under Sections 29A, 30 and 33 of the PEMRA Ordinance, 2002, as amended.The latest notification reiterates the regulator's existing restrictions on live coverage of security incidents, with a focus on verification, editorial checks and the use of broadcast delays.
Article Summary: Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.

Article Title: 6 killed, several injured as passenger train derails in Pakistan's Punjab
Article Text:
Train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan (Representative image) (PTI)

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to prevent train accidents? Improving railway tracks Upgrading safety systems Regular maintenance and inspections 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Article Title: 2 Pakistan army pilots killed as training aircraft crashes near Balochistan's Quetta
Article Text:
2 Pakistan army pilots killed (IANS photo)

Two Pakistan army pilots were killed after a Mushshak training aircraft crashed near Balochistan's Quetta on Monday due to a technical fault, as Dawn reported, citing the ISPR, the official media wing of the Pakistan armed forces.The Pakistan army identified the deceased as Major Husnain Shehzad Humayun, an instructor, and Captain Abdul Samad, a trainee pilot.The aircraft crashed near Nawan Killi in Quetta.In June, a Mi-17 helicopter belonging to the Pakistan army's aviation wing crashed during take-off near Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), reportedly due to a technical fault.All personnel on board were killed.
